opening.headline: When old tool results dominate the context, learn the difference between context editing approaches that remove context according to rules without summarizing, and compression.
body: When an agent opens a file and performs a search, tool results are directly appended to the conversation. Even though results from a single turn are rarely reused in subsequent judgments, they are re-entered every turn. Tokens accumulate rapidly, and irrelevant content disperses the model's focus.

Compression that produces summaries forces the model to generate summaries and may result in loss of detail. This course focuses on context editing—following rules to clear outdated tool outputs and cognitive blocks. It examines symptoms of misaligned settings using concrete examples.
opening.objectivesLead: By the end of this lesson, you will be able to:
objectives: I can describe the method of context editing.
You can distinguish the difference between compression and editing.

screens.title: Old tool results take over the window
screens.lead: Review how the context of an agent that uses many tools is filled. You can compare the sizes of each tool result block in the diagram.

visual.alt: Diagram showing a tool result block accumulating continuously in the conversation, occupying most of the context.
labels: This is all that is needed

paragraphs: When an agent opens a file and performs a search, tool results are directly appended to the conversation. Larger results such as file contents, search outputs, or logs occupy a greater proportion within the context.

The issue is that these results persist even after having been processed. Tool outputs that an agent reads and draws conclusions from during one turn are rarely reused in subsequent judgments. Yet, since previous turn content is re-input each turn, it increases costs and approaches capacity limits. Claude documents explain that irrelevant content can also distract the model's focus.

Compression for summarization is one approach. However, summarization requires the model to generate content and may result in loss of detail. If the content is already processed, such as tool output that has no further value to see, it's simpler to simply remove it according to rules rather than summarize. This is context editing.

callout.label: Things to think about
callout.text: Who should determine whether certain tool results can be left blank, and by what rules should this be decided? This course covers the configuration settings that establish those rules.

screens.outro: First, let me recall your experience.

screens.title: Think about issues arising from tool results being too long
screens.lead: After first thinking through the question mentally and making a choice, the instructor's thought process is revealed. Answers are not entered or submitted.

items.prompt: Has the tool output been long enough to cause issues?
items.answer: It is common for tools to return the entire file or lengthy logs. In such cases, a single result increases the input size for all subsequent turns. The size of tool outputs is one of the most significant factors affecting an agent's cost.

items.prompt: After reading the result, did it continue to remain in the context?
items.answer: Basically, yes. Conversation records accumulate, so results that have been used do not disappear. Therefore, a device intentionally cleared is required.

items.prompt: Have you ever wanted to delete something but not known what exactly could be deleted?
items.answer: This decision is difficult, so an editing policy is needed. We should remove older items while preserving a few recent ones, and never remove essential tools—this approach allows rules to be established that can automate the decision process.

screens.outro: We will examine how this rule is applied by comparing the content before and after editing.

screens.title: Context editing: Counts content according to rules
screens.lead: Switch between the two states to compare how the same conversation differs before and after editing.

visual.alt: Before editing, the original tool output is long; after editing, it is replaced with placeholder text, resulting in a reduced token bar diagram.

states.label: Before editing
states.body: The agent calls tools multiple times, and all results remain in the context as the original input. Even the oldest results, which have already reached a conclusion, are preserved unchanged. This leads to high token counts, increased costs, approaching limits, and distraction of focus with content irrelevant to the current judgment. The conversation history stored by the client is in the same state as what is sent to the model.

states.label: After editing
states.body: Context editing is a method of selectively removing specific content from conversation records. It is not only about cost and limit management but also actively curating the content that the model sees. Server-side editing is applied before the prompt reaches the model, removing older tool results in chronological order and inserting a placeholder indicating that the results have been removed. The client's full record remains unchanged, so there is no need to synchronize with edited records. By default, only tool results are removed; however, if configured, the call input is also removed.

screens.outro: Now we will read the setting that defines tool result removal on a per-line basis.

screens.title: Read Tool Result Removal Setting
screens.lead: Strategy for removing tool results from Claude. Please select the descriptions next to each line to check how the reduction is set and verify the symptoms when values are mismatched.

notes.note: This line selects the strategy of clearing old tool results in chronological order. In the cleared space, a placeholder message indicating "removed" is placed, signaling to the model that the entity has been deleted. The thought block belongs to a different strategy, not this one.

When the prompt exceeds this value, cleanup begins. The default is 100,000 input tokens. If set too high, cleanup will be delayed causing the window to fill up first; if set too low, cleanup will occur excessively, invalidating the cache every time.

The number of recent tool usages and result pairs remaining after summarization. The default value is 3. If it is too small, the agent will treat even the current judgment's rationale as just a placeholder prompt and repeat the same search.

This is the minimum amount that can be evicted at once. There is no default value. If the amount specified is not large enough to justify the eviction, the strategy will not be applied. Each eviction invalidates the cache prefix, so the amount must be large enough to offset that cost.

This tool's invocation and results are protected so they are not erased. Insert a tool that produces results you need to continue referencing. To erase inputs up to the invocation, enable clear_tool_inputs.

screens.outro: There are things that can be organized besides tool results. We will examine the difference between thought blocks and compression.

screens.title: Difference between incident block cleanup and compression
screens.lead: Select each tab to compare the settings for thought block organization and the processing methods for compression and editing.

tabs.label: Incident block cleanup
tabs.body: clear_thinking_20251015 strategy clears thought blocks from the previous assistant turn. Set "keep" to retain recent thought blocks; if set to "all", all thought blocks are retained. Retaining thought blocks keeps the prompt cache active, reducing input costs; removing them invalidates the cache from the point of deletion. Choose whether to prioritize cache performance or creative flexibility when setting "keep".

tabs.label: compression
tabs.body: Compression replaces old content with a summary. Since the model generates the summary anew, summarization incurs costs, and details not included in the summary are lost. Instead, the flow and state of the entire content are preserved through the summary. This approach is appropriate when content must be continuous and it's difficult to determine which parts are unnecessary using rules.

tabs.label: Edit
tabs.body: Editing removes existing content according to rules. Since a new summary is not written, there is no summarization cost. However, the removed content is no longer visible to the model. This is appropriate for removing content that is no longer needed to be viewed, such as results after processing, and if necessary content is removed, the agent will repeat the same task.

tabs.label: write together
tabs.body: You can apply both strategies together. For example, in a request, the reasoning block keeps only the last two turns, while the tool result keeps only the last five entries if the input token count exceeds 50,000. Additionally, when used together with a memory tool, the agent can receive a warning when approaching a summarization threshold and store important content directly into memory first.

screens.outro: Now let's work through an example that reads the configuration and identifies the root cause.

screens.title: Explanation: Edit conversation after 20 search results have been accumulated
screens.lead: The instructor reads the editing settings of a conversation that has accumulated 20 search results, explaining why the agent is repeating the same search. Select the right arrow to proceed.

steps.title: situation
steps.body: The search results accumulate 20 entries, each containing thousands of tokens. The settings are trigger 100000, keep 1, and clear_at_least is not specified. The agent exhibits a symptom of missing the most recent search results and repeatedly performing the same search. The three lines of the configuration are read sequentially to identify the cause.

steps.title: Step 1: Trigger line
steps.body: The trigger value of 100,000 means that processing does not begin until the input reaches this value. Until then, the window continues to be filled with old results, which may lead to the window overflowing or quality degradation depending on the result size. However, this line is not the direct cause of the symptom of repeatedly performing the same search.

steps.title: Step 2: keep line
steps.body: If keep is 1, only the most recent pair of tools used during cleanup remains, and the rest are replaced with placeholder messages. Several of the previous reasons used by the agent are lost, and the agent now only knows that a result occurred. The agent repeatedly performs the same search in an attempt to recover the lost content. This line is the cause of the symptom.

steps.title: Step 3: clear_at_least line
steps.body: If no eviction policy is specified, even a small amount of space being freed triggers cache cleanup. Each time space is freed, the cache prefix becomes invalid, resulting in cache costs being incurred even without actually freeing significant space. Repeated cache write costs reduce the benefits of cleanup.

steps.title: improvement
steps.body: Lower the trigger value in the window to a reasonable level, set keep to around 3, and retain the current justification rationale. Increase clear_at_least to thoroughly clear out old entries, and place tools that need to be continuously referenced into exclude_tools. This way, old results are discarded and recent justifications are preserved.

steps.title: Check effectiveness
steps.body: After making changes to the settings, you verify the effects numerically. The context_management field in the response contains the number of applied edits and the number of unused tool uses, as well as the number of unused input tokens. Additionally, the token calculation feature previews the token count after applying edits, allowing you to compare it with the original token count before the edit and estimate how much it has decreased. This helps confirm that the policy is functioning as intended before sending the actual request.

steps.title: Instructor's judgment
steps.body: The criterion for removal is that results already reflected in the answer may be removed, while results to be seen again in the future should be retained. This criterion translated into numerical form is the editing policy. After policy changes, the consolidated content and token count are confirmed in the response's context_management field.

screens.outro: Finally, let's summarize the key points.

screens.title: Key takeaway: Unused tool results are pruned
screens.lead: We organize the criteria for context editing.

paragraphs: Unnecessary tool outputs are removed. Editing replaces existing content according to rules, while compression replaces content with a new summary. Editing is appropriate for content that is no longer needed to review after processing, whereas compression is suitable for content that must flow continuously. Both strategies can be used together.

The cleanup policy consists of four values: trigger determines when cleanup begins, keep specifies the number of most recent entries to retain, clear_at_least defines the minimum amount to clear at once, and exclude_tools specifies which tools to protect. If these values are misaligned, cleanup may be delayed, causing the window to become full, the current justification to disappear, or resulting in only cache costs being incurred.

The starting point is simple: determine which tool in your agent produces the most impactful results, and then assess whether those results are still needed in the next turn. If not, that tool becomes a primary target for editing policy. After defining the policy, actually run through the process again to verify whether work continues beyond the cleanup phase. If issues arise, adjust the keep and exclude_tools settings first.

callout.label: something to remember
callout.text: Editing is simpler than summarizing, but once content is deleted, it cannot be recovered. Determining what to keep and what tools to protect is at the core of policy.

glossary.def: It is the process of selectively omitting specific content from conversation records according to rules, curating the content that the model sees.
This strategy replaces the token with a placeholder statement indicating that the processing of old tool results is complete.
A strategy of either clearing or retaining a certain number of thought blocks from the previous turn.
Rule defining when and how much to delete, based on settings such as trigger, keep, clear_at_least, and exclude_tools.

misconceptions.myth: Editing is another name for compression.
misconceptions.fact: Compression replaces summary with a new one, while editing erases existing content according to rules. The difference lies in whether summary cost is considered and whether the erased content can be observed.

misconceptions.myth: Deleting it also removes the client record.
misconceptions.fact: Server-side editing is applied before the prompt reaches the model. The client's entire conversation history remains unchanged.

misconceptions.myth: The more frequently you delete it, the better.
misconceptions.fact: The cache prefix may become invalid each time it is cleared, so it only provides benefits when thoroughly emptied. clear_at_least is used to specify the minimum clearing amount.

closing.lead: Summarizes what was covered in this class.
points: Unnecessary tool results are removed according to rules.
Editing removes according to rules and compression replaces with summarization.
trigger, keep, clear_at_least, exclude_tools compose the editing policy.
Policy values define the retention point, retention amount, and exceptions.
